newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: Randgold sees longer life for Mali mine.
newsitem.headline: Randgold sees longer life for Mali mine.

text.p: Randgold Resources said on Wednesday it had improved productivity of Mali's Syama mine by 25 percent over the last month and expected to be able to extend its life beyond the currently projected nine years.

Managing director Mark Bristow told an African mining conference, "Having managed the operation for four months now, we are happy that our due diligence identified all the critical issues, none of which are unsolvable.

"It will take some time or money to realise the full benefit of the re-engineering process. However, I have confidence that the plan in place will result in the optimum exploitation of the ore body," he said.
Randgold was confident of being able to increase the life of the mine beyond its current nine years.
"It is also well situated to serve as a hub for resources expansion and the growth of projects in west Africa," he said.
Randgold Resources acquired management control and 65 percent of the share capital of Syama gold mine in Mali as part of its acquisition of BHP Mali Inc in October 1996.
The mine had been dogged by poor technical decisions and tensions between management and workers.
The main deposit consists of some 3.9 million ounces down to 450 metres below surface plus shallow resources in three other areas.
Bristow said Randgold had identified a further 23 targets which would be the focus of its exploration programme over the next three years.

It had, however, developed a reputation as a project with a metallurgically difficult rock and complex labour problems. During Randgold's due diligence, it had identified major problem areas as being poor drill and blast practices as well as grade management.
"Syama has shown a dramatic improvement in grade management since October 1996," he said.

"Over the past month we have seen up to a 25 percent improvement in mining productivity which can be attributed to the improvement in drill and blast practices, an increase in bench heights and changed operating shifts from two 12 hour shifts to three eight hour shifts."

In the processing plant, the biggest mistakes had been the choice of technical processes. For example the crusher did not allow for direct discharge by dump trucks, which meant that there had to be costly re-handling of ore. A new crusher had now arrived on site and would be installed over the next nine months.
In addition, the administration offices had been moved from Bumako, which was a five hours' drive away, to the mine.
Bristow said good progress had been made on negotiations towards a mine-based labour agreement.
